prompt: The new checkout converted 4.67% and the old 4.28%. What is the difference in percentage points?
hint: The program's +0.40 comes from unrounded rates.

prompt: A control converts at 4.00% and a treatment at 4.40%. What is the relative lift, in per cent?
Which of these is the most complete way to report a test's result?

choices.why: A relative lift and a word hide the counts and the uncertainty.

choices.text: Counts, rates, the difference with its interval, and the test
choices.why: Right.
A p-value alone says nothing about size.

choices.text: The conversion of the treatment group, since that is the version the business will ship
choices.why: Without the control there is nothing to compare.

prompt: Why compare the control's observed rate, 4.28%, with the 4.2% the plan assumed?

choices.why: Right. Here they are close, so the power was as designed.
That compares the two groups, not the control with the plan.

choices.text: To detect a sample ratio mismatch
choices.why: That compares group sizes, not rates.

choices.text: It must be exactly equal for the test to be valid, or the result has to be thrown away
choices.why: Some difference is normal; it changes the power, not the validity.

prompt: Panela's test gave p = 0.032. What does that mean?

choices.text: There is a 3.2% chance the new page is no better
choices.why: That is the common backwards reading; it needs a prior the test does not have.
A p-value is not an effect size.

choices.text: 96.8% of visitors prefer the new page
choices.why: Nothing in a p-value is about preferences.

choices.text: If the pages converted equally, a gap this large would occur about 3 times in 100
choices.why: Right.

prompt: The 95% interval for the lift is +0.03 to +0.76 points. Which statement does it support?

choices.why: That is the point estimate; the interval says how sure it is.

choices.text: The lift is at least the planned 0.6 points
choices.why: Most of the interval is below 0.6.

choices.text: Probably better, by between almost nothing and three quarters of a point
choices.why: Right.
Zero is outside the interval.

prompt: A huge test finds a lift of 0.01 points with p = 0.0001. What should a manager conclude?

choices.text: A major win, since p is so small
choices.why: p is small because the test is huge.

choices.text: Real, and too small to matter
choices.why: Right. Significance is not importance.
Nothing is broken; big tests see small effects.
That is not a quantity anybody uses.

prompt: Match where an interval sits to its reading.

pairs.right: real and large enough to matter

pairs.left: above zero, reaching below the MDE
around zero, reaching above the MDE

prompt: Two tests both report 'no significant difference'. One interval is −0.1 to +0.2 points, the other −0.3 to +0.9, with an MDE of 0.6. How do they differ?

choices.text: Only the first is an answer
choices.why: Right. It depends on whether the interval reaches the MDE.

choices.text: They do not; both found nothing
choices.why: One answered the question and the other could not.

choices.text: The second is closer to significance, so it should be run a little longer until it gets there
choices.why: Extending until significant is peeking, lesson 11's subject.
The first is the precise one.

prompt: Which case is Panela's weeks-2-and-3 result, −0.36 to +0.51 against an MDE of 0.6?

choices.why: It includes zero.
It includes zero, so not shown to be real.
Its top end nearly reaches the MDE, so it cannot rule out a useful effect.
Right. Close enough to the MDE that a useful effect is not ruled out.

prompt: The plan said ship if significant at 5%. The test is significant, but the late weeks look flat. What does the lesson recommend?

choices.text: Do not ship, since the late weeks are what matters
choices.why: That changes the rule after seeing the data.
Rerunning until the answer is clearer is fishing.

choices.text: Ship as planned, say the lasting effect is probably smaller, and track it after launch
choices.why: Right. Follow the rule, and name the doubt.
That hides the most important caveat.

prompt: What lasting lift did panela.py build into the new checkout?

choices.why: That is the weeks-2-and-3 estimate, pulled down by noise.
Right, plus a novelty bonus that fades.
That is where the novelty bonus starts.
That is the plan's MDE.

prompt: Why is declaring a bigger win because week 1 looks great just as wrong as declaring a loss because weeks 2 and 3 look flat?

choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Week 1 and weeks 2 and 3 have the same number of visitors
choices.why: They do not, and that is not the point.
Weeks 2 and 3 alone are not.
The test is the same; the choice of what to read is the problem.

prompt: Why do significant results from small tests tend to overstate the effect?

choices.text: Small tests use a bigger α
choices.why: α is the same; the selection does the damage.

choices.text: Small companies exaggerate their results in reports, more than large companies do
choices.why: It is arithmetic, not honesty.

choices.text: Novelty is larger in small tests
choices.why: Novelty is a separate effect.

choices.text: Only the runs that happened to estimate high cross the line
choices.why: Right. Selection by significance favours overestimates.

prompt: A test barely crossed the significance line. Which number makes a sober planning estimate?

choices.text: The upper end of the interval
choices.why: That is the most optimistic reading.
In a just-significant test it is likely too high.

choices.text: The lower end of the interval
choices.why: Right.
The MDE is a planning threshold, not an estimate.

prompt: Put the steps of reading a test result in order.
items: check the split and the balance
compute rates, difference, interval and p
read the interval against zero and the MDE
look at the effect over time
apply the rule written in the plan

prompt: The range of true effects the data is compatible with is the ___ interval.
